objectives: Compute period net cash flow and the running cumulative cash position from inflow and outflow data
Identify peak funding as the deepest cumulative deficit, expressed as a positive funding requirement
Interpret the closing cumulative position as the project's net cash outcome over the reporting window

Step 1 — Net cash flow per period: net = inflow − outflow.
P1: 0 − 40 = −40
P2: 20 − 50 = −30
P3: 60 − 45 = +15
P4: 70 − 40 = +30
P5: 80 − 35 = +45
P6: 60 − 30 = +30

After P1: −40

After P3: −70 + 15 = −55  ← cumulative position at end of period 3
After P4: −55 + 30 = −25

Step 4 — Final position: the closing cumulative net after period 6 is +50.

Answers: cumulative_3 = −55; peak_funding = 70; final_position = 50.

scenarios.title: Coastal Shield Landing Craft Mid-Life Upgrade — Cost Breakdown Roll-Up
scenarios.project_type: amphibious landing craft mid-life upgrade programme
scenarios.summary: Roll up a defence refit cost breakdown structure, compute programme-level actuals and variance, and isolate a hidden favourable variance the sponsor has overlooked.
scenarios.brief: You are the cost controller on Programme Coastal Shield, a mid-life upgrade of a fleet of amphibious landing craft. The refit yard has just submitted period actuals, and the programme sponsor is alarmed by headline overspend chatter from the hull shop. Before the steering board meets, you must roll the cost breakdown structure up from leaf work packages to programme level and show where money is truly being lost — and where one work package is quietly returning budget.
objectives: Compute roll-up totals for budget and actual cost from leaf work packages to the programme root of a CBS.
Compute cost variance (budget minus actual) at leaf, parent, and root levels.
Distinguish an unfavourable (overspend) variance from a favourable (opportunity) variance within the same structure.
Interpret a parent-level variance as the sum of its children's variances rather than a directly booked value.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the budget. Only leaves carry values: 1.1.1 (4200) + 1.1.2 (1800) + 1.2 (6500) + 1.3 (3900) + 1.4 (1600) = 18000. Parent 1.1 budget = 4200 + 1800 = 6000.

Step 2 — Roll up the actuals (root_actual). 1.1.1 (4650) + 1.1.2 (2140) + 1.2 (7020) + 1.3 (3510) + 1.4 (1750) = 19070. So root_actual = 19070.00.

Step 3 — Programme variance (root_variance). Variance = budget − actual = 18000 − 19070 = −1070. So root_variance = −1070.00, an overall overspend.

Step 4 — Parent-level variance for Hull & Structural Refurbishment (variance_1.1). Node 1.1 carries no booked values of its own; roll up its children. Budget = 6000; actual = 4650 + 2140 = 6790. Variance = 6000 − 6790 = −790.00. Equivalently, sum the children's variances: (4200 − 4650) + (1800 − 2140) = −450 + (−340) = −790.

Step 5 — Leaf variance for Propulsion Overhaul (variance_1.3). Variance = 3900 − 3510 = +390.00. This is the favourable variance (opportunity): despite the programme's net overspend of 1070, the propulsion work package is returning 390 of budget, which partly offsets the hull and combat-systems overruns.

Final answers: root_actual = 19070.00; root_variance = −1070.00; variance_1.1 = −790.00; variance_1.3 = 390.00.

scenarios.brief: A regional hospital is refurbishing its sterile processing department so surgical instrument turnaround can keep pace with a new operating theatre. The works were split into four cost packages: washer-disinfector replacement, clean-room partitioning, an instrument-tracking system, and technician training. objectives: Compute the total budget of a cost breakdown structure by rolling up leaf-level budgets to the root

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Roll up the budget. The root budget is the sum of the four leaf budgets: 42000 + 30000 + 18000 + 10000 = 100000. So root_budget = 100000.

Step 2 — Roll up the actuals. The root actual is the sum of the four leaf actuals: 45500 + 28000 + 19200 + 9300 = 102000. So root_actual = 102000.

Step 3 — Compute the cost variance. Variance = budget - actual = 100000 - 102000 = -2000. So root_variance = -2000.

Interpretation: the negative variance means the project finished 2000 over budget. Checking the leaves shows why: the washer-disinfector package overran by 3500 (42000 - 45500) and instrument tracking by 1200, while partitioning saved 2000 and training saved 700 — savings that only partly offset the equipment overrun the sponsor was worried about.

scenarios.title: Change Control at the Millbrook Reclamation Works Membrane Retrofit
scenarios.project_type: membrane filtration retrofit at a water reclamation plant
scenarios.summary: Work a live change register for a water reclamation plant retrofit: sort approved, pending, and rejected changes, then compute the revised BAC and revised duration from approved changes only.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls lead on a membrane filtration retrofit at a regional water reclamation works. The sponsor is nervous: the change register has grown fast this month, one big remediation request is still with the change board, and an operations manager has been telling site staff that a SCADA upgrade is "signed off" when the board actually rejected it. Before Thursday's steering committee you must restate the performance measurement baseline using only changes formally approved by the change board.
objectives: Distinguish approved changes from pending and rejected changes when restating a baseline
Compute the approved cost delta and approved schedule delta from a change register
Compute the revised BAC and revised duration by applying only approved changes
Interpret an approved opportunity (negative delta) correctly within a register of threats

scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real utility, plant, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures:

Step 1 — Screen the register by status. Only changes with status "approved" move the baseline. C1 (UV disinfection channel, +185000 cost, +3 weeks), C3 (pre-cast chlorine contact tank, -60000 cost, -2 weeks), and C5 (dewatering allowance, +38000 cost, +1 week) are approved. C2 (pipe gallery corrosion remediation, +240000, +4) is still pending — it is tempting because everyone expects it to pass, but it has not, so it is excluded. C4 (SCADA upgrade, +95000, +2) was rejected by the change board despite the operations manager's verbal "sign-off" — excluded.

Step 2 — Approved cost delta = sum of approved cost deltas = 185000 + (-60000) + 38000 = 163000. Note the approved opportunity C3 reduces the total; do not drop it just because it is negative.

Step 3 — Approved schedule delta = 3 + (-2) + 1 = 2 weeks.

Step 4 — Revised BAC = baseline BAC + approved cost delta = 4200000 + 163000 = 4363000.

Step 5 — Revised duration = baseline duration + approved schedule delta = 40 + 2 = 42 weeks.

Final answers: approved_cost_delta = 163000; approved_schedule_delta = 2; revised_bac = 4363000; revised_duration = 42.

scenarios.title: Earned Schedule Check on a Drought-Resilience Intake Upgrade
scenarios.summary: Interpolate earned schedule from a cumulative PV curve for a water intake upgrade, strip out a rejected change from reported EV, and forecast time-based completion with SPI(t).
scenarios.brief: A regional utility is upgrading its raw-water intake and pre-treatment works as part of a drought-resilience program: a new low-level intake screen, twin sedimentation basins, and an interconnecting gravity main. The 8-month baseline is under pressure after river access restrictions slowed basin excavation. At the month-5 review, the contractor's progress report includes a scope change the change board actually rejected, so you must validate earned value before running the earned-schedule analysis the steering group has asked for.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by linear interpolation between two periods of a cumulative planned-value curve
Distinguish approved earned value from claimed earned value that includes a rejected change
Compute time-based schedule variance SV(t) and performance index SPI(t) from ES and actual time
Forecast a time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) using planned duration and SPI(t)
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, utility, or contractor.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Validate EV. The contractor's month-5 report claims cumulative earned value of 228, but this includes 28 earned against change request CR-14, which the change board REJECTED (the contractor's log is out of date). Validated EV = 228 - 28 = 200.

Step 2 — Earned schedule (ES). Find where EV = 200 sits on the cumulative PV curve. PV(3) = 160 and PV(4) = 240, so 160 < 200 < 240 and ES lies between periods 3 and 4. Interpolate: ES = 3 + (EV - PV(3)) / (PV(4) - PV(3)) = 3 + (200 - 160) / (240 - 160) = 3 + 40/80 = 3.50 months.

Step 3 — Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.50 - 5 = -1.50 months. The project has earned only 3.5 months of the plan in 5 months of work — 1.5 months behind.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.50 / 5 = 0.70.

Step 5 — Time-based estimate at completion. EAC(t) = planned_duration / SPI(t) = 8 / 0.70 = 11.4286 ≈ 11.43 months, versus the 8-month baseline — about 3.4 months of forecast slip if performance does not improve.

Final answers: ES = 3.50; SV(t) = -1.50; SPI(t) = 0.70; EAC(t) = 11.43.

config.prompt: You are the project controls analyst on a regional utility's drought-resilience intake upgrade (new low-level intake screen, twin sedimentation basins, interconnecting gravity main), baselined at 8 months. Cumulative planned value by month: 40, 95, 160, 240, 330, 420, 490, 540 (final cumulative PV 540). It is the end of month 5 (AT = 5). The contractor reports cumulative earned value of 228, but that figure includes 28 earned against change request CR-14, which the change board rejected; only board-approved scope may earn value. Using the validated earned value, compute: 1) es — earned schedule ES, in months, interpolating linearly between the two months of the cumulative PV curve that bracket the validated EV; 2) sv_time — time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT, in months; 3) spi_time — schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT; 4) eac_time — time-based estimate at completion EAC(t) = planned duration / SPI(t), in months. Round all answers, including indices, to 2 decimal places.

scenarios.worked_solution: For the canonical figures: Cumulative PV curve is 100, 250, 450, 700, 900, 1000 over periods 1-6; AT = 4; EV = 350. Step 1 - locate EV on the PV curve: EV = 350 lies between PV(2) = 250 and PV(3) = 450, so ES is between periods 2 and 3. Step 2 - interpolate: ES = 2 + (EV - PV(2)) / (PV(3) - PV(2)) = 2 + (350 - 250) / (450 - 250) = 2 + 100/200 = 2.50 periods. Step 4 - time-based index: SPI(t) = ES / AT = 2.50 / 4 = 0.625, rounded to 0.63, confirming the project is progressing at roughly 63% of the planned rate. (For reference, a time forecast would be EAC(t) = planned_duration / SPI(t) = 6 / 0.625 = 9.6 periods.) Final answers: ES = 2.50, SV(t) = -1.50, SPI(t) = 0.63.

scenarios.title: Footbridge Frame: First EVM Health Check
scenarios.summary: A prefabricated timber footbridge project is spending faster than it is earning. Compute SV, CV, and CPI from a single monthly snapshot to size the problem for the sponsor.
scenarios.brief: You are the junior project controller on a prefabricated cross-laminated timber footbridge being erected across a drainage canal. Wet weather has slowed panel deliveries, and the erection crane has been kept on standby at full day rate, so costs are running ahead of the work actually installed. The sponsor has asked for a one-page variance summary before approving the next drawdown, and you must produce the core earned value figures from this month's snapshot.
objectives: Compute schedule variance (SV) and cost variance (CV) from a single EVM snapshot
Compute the cost performance index (CPI) and round it to 2 decimal places
Interpret negative variances as behind-schedule and over-budget signals for a sponsor briefing
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real project, company, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 400, EV = 360, AC = 450, BAC = 1200.

Step 1 — Schedule Variance: SV = EV − PV = 360 − 400 = −40. The project has earned 40 less than planned for this point, so it is behind schedule.

Step 2 — Cost Variance: CV = EV − AC = 360 − 450 = −90. The work earned cost 90 more than its budgeted value, confirming the sponsor's overspend concern.

Step 3 — Cost Performance Index: CPI = EV / AC = 360 / 450 = 0.80 (2 decimal places). Every unit spent is returning only 0.80 of budgeted work — the crane standby costs are eroding cost efficiency.

Final answers: SV = −40, CV = −90, CPI = 0.80.

scenarios.title: Busway Viaduct Overspend: CPI Forecast Under a Rejected Change
scenarios.summary: Month-8 cost health check on an elevated busway viaduct: compute CV, CPI, a CPI-based EAC, and VAC — while spotting that a rejected change request must not inflate the baseline.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a 4.2 km elevated busway viaduct programme at its month-8 status snapshot. Girder erection has fallen behind the launch sequence while night-shift premiums and crane standby charges have pushed spending up, and the sponsor wants a defensible forecast before the next steering committee. Complicating matters, the contractor's monthly report presents change request CR-17 (value 60000, for utility relocation) as if it were approved — but the change board rejected it, so the performance measurement baseline is unchanged.
objectives: Compute cost variance and the cost performance index from a single EVM status snapshot
Forecast estimate at completion using the CPI-based method (EAC = BAC / CPI)
Compute variance at completion and interpret its sign for sponsor reporting
Distinguish a rejected change request from an approved baseline change when selecting BAC
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or contract.
scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 300000, EV = 264000, AC = 292000, BAC = 720000. Change request CR-17 (60000) was rejected by the change board, so BAC remains 720000 — do not add CR-17 to any figure.

Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 264000 - 292000 = -28000. Negative, so the work performed cost more than its earned budget.

Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 264000 / 292000 = 0.90411... ≈ 0.90 (2 dp). Each unit spent is earning about 0.90 of value.

Step 3 — Estimate at completion (current cost performance continues): EAC = BAC / CPI = 720000 / 0.90411 = 796363.64. Use the unrounded CPI here — dividing by the rounded 0.90 would give 800000 and overstate the forecast.

Step 4 — Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 720000 - 796363.64 = -76363.64. A negative VAC means the project is forecast to finish about 76363.64 over budget if cost efficiency does not improve — the figure the sponsor needs for the steering committee.

Key trap: had you treated CR-17 as approved and used BAC = 780000, every forecast figure would be wrong. Only board-approved changes move the performance measurement baseline.

scenarios.title: Coastal Radar Mid-Life Upgrade — Cost Pressure at the Integration Gate
scenarios.project_type: Naval coastal surveillance radar mid-life upgrade
scenarios.summary: A defence radar mid-life upgrade is overspending during antenna integration while a rejected scope change still inflates the contractor's dashboard budget. Compute variances, CPI, EAC and VAC from the true baseline.
scenarios.brief: You are the project controls analyst on a mid-life upgrade of a coastal surveillance radar chain: replacing the transmitter cabinets, re-blading the signal processors, and re-certifying the array on a live naval site. At the current reporting snapshot the integration work is running behind and over cost, and the sponsor wants a forecast before the next gate review. Complicating matters, the contractor's dashboard shows a budget that includes change request CR-114 (a 5000 uplift for spare transmitter modules) — but the change board REJECTED CR-114 last week, so the approved budget at completion remains as originally baselined.
objectives: Compute cost variance and CPI from a single EVM snapshot
Compute a CPI-based estimate at completion and the variance at completion
Distinguish the approved budget at completion from an unapproved (rejected) change-inflated figure
Interpret an unfavourable cost trend for a sponsor-facing gate review
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real programme, contractor, or defence organisation.
scenarios.worked_solution: For the canonical figures: PV = 15600, EV = 14100, AC = 16400, BAC = 42000. Note the twist first: CR-114 was rejected, so the dashboard figure of 47000 is NOT the budget — use the approved BAC of 42000 throughout. Step 1 — Cost variance: CV = EV - AC = 14100 - 16400 = -2300. Work performed has cost 2300 more than it earned. Step 2 — Cost performance index: CPI = EV / AC = 14100 / 16400 = 0.8598..., which rounds to 0.86. Every unit spent is earning about 0.86 of value. Step 3 — CPI-based estimate at completion: EAC = BAC / CPI. Use the unrounded CPI (equivalently EAC = BAC × AC / EV) = 42000 × 16400 / 14100 = 48851.06. Step 4 — Variance at completion: VAC = BAC - EAC = 42000 - 48851.06 = -6851.06. Interpretation for the gate review: with SPI = 14100/15600 = 0.90 and CPI = 0.86, the project is behind schedule and over cost; if current cost efficiency persists, the upgrade will finish roughly 6851 over the approved baseline — and quoting the rejected-CR figure of 47000 would understate the overrun the sponsor actually faces.

scenarios.summary: Track six months of cumulative earned value on a hospital hybrid theatre fit-out, isolate the worst schedule month, and forecast completion cost while ignoring a rejected change order.
scenarios.brief: A 400-bed teaching hospital is converting two conventional theatres into a single hybrid operating suite with integrated interventional imaging. Radiation-shielding rework and delayed ceiling-gantry deliveries have rattled the clinical steering group, and the fit-out contractor's latest forecast quietly assumes a shielding change order that the change board actually rejected. You are the project controls analyst asked to give the sponsor a clean, evidence-based read of schedule history and cost outlook.
objectives: Compute cumulative CPI from period earned value data and round indices to two decimal places
Forecast EAC using the CPI-based formula EAC = BAC / final CPI and derive VAC
Distinguish approved baseline scope from a rejected change order when selecting the BAC
Interpret a timeline of SPI values to identify the single worst schedule performance month
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real hospital, vendor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Fix the BAC. The 350 shielding change order was REJECTED by the change board, so it never enters the baseline. BAC stays 4200.

Step 2 — Per-period indices (SPI = EV/PV, CPI = EV/AC, cumulative values):
P1: SPI = 380/400 = 0.95; CPI = 380/390 = 0.97
P2: SPI = 820/900 = 0.91; CPI = 820/860 = 0.95
P3: SPI = 1260/1500 = 0.84; CPI = 1260/1380 = 0.91
P4: SPI = 1850/2100 = 0.88; CPI = 1850/2160 = 0.86
P5: SPI = 2550/2800 = 0.91; CPI = 2550/2890 = 0.88
P6: SPI = 3120/3400 = 0.92; CPI = 3120/3480 = 0.90

Worst SPI month is Period 3 (0.84 — the gantry delivery slip); worst CPI month is Period 4 (0.86 — the shielding rework peak). Neither is the final period, and each minimum is unique.

Step 3 — Final CPI = final EV / final AC = 3120 / 3480 = 0.8966, reported as 0.90 (2 dp).

Step 4 — EAC = BAC / final CPI = 4200 / (3120/3480) = 4200 x 3480 / 3120 = 4684.62.

Step 5 — VAC = BAC - EAC = 4200 - 4684.62 = -484.62. The negative VAC quantifies the overspend the sponsor is worried about: at current cost efficiency the fit-out finishes about 485 over the approved baseline.

Answers: final_cpi = 0.90; final_eac = 4684.62; vac = -484.62; worst_spi_period = 3.

scenarios.title: Weighted Progress at the Reedmarsh Sludge Dewatering Upgrade
scenarios.summary: Roll up work-package percent complete into a single weighted progress figure for a water treatment sludge dewatering upgrade, and see why the sponsor's "it looks 75% done" impression is misleading.
scenarios.brief: The Reedmarsh water treatment works is replacing its ageing belt presses with two new centrifuge dewatering trains. The civil enabling works finished quickly and the site looks well advanced, so the programme sponsor believes the job is about three-quarters complete. As the project controls analyst, you must weight each work package by its budget share and report the true overall percent complete before the next steering meeting.
objectives: Compute overall percent complete as a budget-weighted average of work-package progress
Compute the total weighting basis used to normalise the roll-up
Interpret why unweighted or visual impressions of progress can overstate true completion
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, company, or site.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Confirm the weighting basis. Total weight = 40 + 25 + 15 + 12 + 8 = 100.

Step 2 — Multiply each work package's weight by its percent complete:
- 1.1 Civil enabling works: 40 x 90 = 3600
- 1.2 Centrifuge train A installation: 25 x 60 = 1500
- 1.3 Centrifuge train B installation: 15 x 40 = 600
- 1.4 Polymer dosing system: 12 x 25 = 300
- 1.5 Commissioning and handover: 8 x 0 = 0

Step 3 — Sum the weighted contributions: 3600 + 1500 + 600 + 300 + 0 = 6000.

Step 4 — Divide by the total weight: overall percent complete = 6000 / 100 = 60.00%.

Interpretation: although the site visually looks about 75% done because the heavily weighted civil package is at 90%, the mechanical, dosing, and commissioning packages drag the true budget-weighted progress down to 60.00%. Total weight = 100.

scenarios.summary: Run a forward and backward pass on a six-activity tug fit-out network to find the project duration, the critical path, and the total float on the electrical branch.
scenarios.brief: A mid-size yard is fitting out a 28 m harbour tug at its outfitting berth, and the delivery date hinges on two work fronts that split after the hull modules are joined: a mechanical branch (piping, then engine room outfit) and an electrical branch (cable pulls, then wheelhouse console). Both branches must finish before commissioning trials can start. The berth planner has asked you to run the critical path calculation so the yard knows which branch drives the delivery date and how much slack the other branch really has.
objectives: Compute early and late dates for a small activity network using forward and backward passes
Identify the critical path and the overall project duration of a fit-out sequence
Compute total float for a non-critical activity and interpret it as schedule slack

scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training; they do not represent any real yard, vessel, or schedule.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Forward pass (ES = max EF of predecessors; EF = ES + dur). A: ES 0, EF 4. B (after A): ES 4, EF 10. C (after A): ES 4, EF 7. D (after B): ES 10, EF 15. E (after C): ES 7, EF 11. F (after D and E): ES = max(15, 11) = 15, EF 18. Project duration = 18 days.

Step 2 — Backward pass (LF = min LS of successors; LS = LF - dur). F: LF 18, LS 15. D: LF 15, LS 10. E: LF 15, LS 11. B: LF 10, LS 4. C: LF = LS of E = 11, LS 8. A: LF = min(LS B, LS C) = min(4, 8) = 4, LS 0.

Step 3 — Total float (TF = LS - ES). A: 0, B: 0, D: 0, F: 0 — these form the critical path A → B → D → F. C: TF = 8 - 4 = 4. E: TF = 11 - 7 = 4.

Answers: project_duration = 18; critical_path = {A, B, D, F}; float_C = 4 days. Interpretation: the electrical branch (C, E) can slip up to 4 days in total before it delays commissioning trials; the mechanical branch has no slack.

scenarios.title: Kestrel Vale Bypass: Earned Schedule After a Rejected Variation
scenarios.summary: A bypass programme's dashboard flatters progress with a rejected drainage variation. Strip it out, interpolate earned schedule at month 6, and forecast the true completion date with SPI(t).
scenarios.brief: The Kestrel Vale Bypass is a 9.5 km single-carriageway highway realignment with three roundabouts and a wildlife green bridge, planned over a 10-month earthworks-to-surfacing programme. At the end of month 6 the delivery partner's dashboard claims cumulative earned value of 3000, but the project controls office has flagged that 250 of that claim relates to a drainage realignment variation whose change request was formally REJECTED at the last change board — it only looks approved on the dashboard. The sponsor wants a time-based (earned schedule) view of progress before the surfacing subcontract is locked in.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by linear interpolation between cumulative planned-value periods
Distinguish approved baseline scope from rejected change work when establishing earned value
Compute time-based schedule metrics SV(t) and SPI(t) at a status date
Forecast total project duration using EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) and interpret the slippage
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real project, organisation, or location.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Correct the earned value. The dashboard claims EV = 3000, but 250 of that belongs to a drainage realignment variation whose change request was rejected; it is not baseline scope. Corrected EV = 3000 - 250 = 2750.

Step 2 — Locate EV on the cumulative PV curve. PV(4) = 2300 and PV(5) = 3200, so 2300 < 2750 < 3200: ES lies between months 4 and 5.

Step 3 — Interpolate ES. ES = 4 + (EV - PV(4)) / (PV(5) - PV(4)) = 4 + (2750 - 2300) / (3200 - 2300) = 4 + 450/900 = 4.50 months.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 4.50 - 6 = -1.50 months. The project has earned only 4.5 months of planned progress in 6 elapsed months: 1.5 months behind.

Step 5 — Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 4.50 / 6 = 0.75.

Step 6 — Time forecast at completion. EAC(t) = PD / SPI(t) = 10 / 0.75 = 13.33 months, i.e. roughly 3.3 months of forecast slippage against the 10-month baseline if current schedule performance persists.

Final answers: es = 4.50; sv_time = -1.50; spi_time = 0.75; eac_time = 13.33.

scenarios.title: Grandstand on the Clock: Earned Schedule at the Harbour Arena
scenarios.summary: Convert cost-based progress data into time-based measures for a six-week demountable grandstand build: interpolate earned schedule, then derive SV(t) and SPI(t) at the week-4 status point.
scenarios.brief: Coastline Events has erected a six-week demountable grandstand programme for a pop-up beach volleyball arena on a reclaimed harbour lot: scaffold towers, seating decks, camera gantries and egress stairs, all planned against a cumulative weekly planned-value curve. At the end of week 4 the site team reports earned value of 360 against a total planned value of 600, and the venue director wants a time-based read on progress because the broadcast rights holder has a fixed rehearsal date. Your job is to convert the cost-denominated data into earned schedule measures.
objectives: Compute earned schedule (ES) by interpolating earned value against a cumulative planned-value curve
Compute the time-based schedule variance SV(t) = ES - AT and state its sign convention
Compute and interpret the time-based schedule performance index SPI(t) = ES / AT
scenarios.provenance: Authored synthetically for the PCI Simulation Lab content library, 2026.
scenarios.disclaimers: All figures are synthetic and simplified for training purposes; they do not represent any real venue, contractor, or project.
scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 - Locate EV on the cumulative PV curve. EV = 360. The plan shows PV(3) = 300 and PV(4) = 420, so 300 < 360 <= 420 and ES lies between week 3 and week 4.

Step 2 - Interpolate ES. ES = C + (EV - PV(C)) / (PV(C+1) - PV(C)), where C = 3 is the last whole period with PV <= EV.
ES = 3 + (360 - 300) / (420 - 300) = 3 + 60/120 = 3 + 0.50 = 3.50 weeks.

Step 3 - Time-based schedule variance. SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.50 - 4 = -0.50 weeks. The negative sign means the work earned by the end of week 4 was planned to be complete half a week earlier than has actually elapsed - the build is running about half a week behind plan.

Step 4 - Time-based schedule performance index. SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.50 / 4 = 0.875, which rounds to 0.88 to 2 decimal places. An SPI(t) below 1.00 confirms the programme is progressing slower than planned in time terms.

Final answers: ES = 3.50 weeks; SV(t) = -0.50 weeks; SPI(t) = 0.88 (0.875 unrounded).

Forecast completion cost using EAC = BAC / CPI and derive the variance at completion
Compute TCPI against BAC and interpret the required cost efficiency to recover

scenarios.worked_solution:
For the canonical figures: PV = 736,000; EV = 662,400; AC = 745,200; BAC = 1,840,000.

Step 0 — Select the right budget. CR-014 (150,000) was REJECTED by the change board, so BAC remains 1,840,000. Do not inflate BAC.

Step 1 — CPI = EV / AC = 662,400 / 745,200 = 0.8888... ≈ 0.89. Each unit spent is earning about 0.89 of value: a cost overrun.

Rounding: indices (CPI, TCPI) to 2 decimal places; money values (EAC, VAC) to the nearest whole number.

scenarios.summary: Run a PERT analysis on a five-activity liquid-cooling retrofit chain in a live data hall and estimate the probability of hitting a contractual re-energisation deadline that a rejected change request tried to move.
scenarios.brief: A colocation operator is converting Hall C from air cooling to direct liquid cooling so a hyperscale tenant can deploy high-density compute racks. The retrofit runs as a strict five-activity chain because the hall's chilled-water loop must stay isolated until commissioning completes. The tenant's hosting agreement sets a re-energisation deadline of 52 working days; a subcontractor's change request to relax it to 56 days is stamped "logged" in the weekly report but was formally REJECTED by the change board, so the 52-day date stands. The delivery director wants a defensible probability of finishing on time before the next tenant review.
objectives: Compute PERT expected durations from three-point (o, m, p) estimates and aggregate them along an activity chain.
Compute the chain standard deviation by summing activity variances, not standard deviations.
Interpret a z-score against the normal distribution to estimate the probability of meeting a deadline.
Distinguish the governing contractual deadline from a rejected change request that appears in project reporting.

scenarios.worked_solution:
Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p)/6:
A Drain and isolate chilled-water loop: (4 + 24 + 10)/6 = 6.33
B Install CDU skids: (8 + 40 + 14)/6 = 10.33
C Pipework and manifold tie-ins: (10 + 52 + 22)/6 = 14.00
D Leak test and fluid charge: (5 + 28 + 12)/6 = 7.50
E Integrated systems commissioning: (6 + 36 + 15)/6 = 9.50

Step 2 — Chain expected duration: E = 6.33 + 10.33 + 14.00 + 7.50 + 9.50 = 47.67 days.

Step 3 — Variance per activity, v = ((p - o)/6)^2:
A: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; B: (6/6)^2 = 1.0000; C: (12/6)^2 = 4.0000; D: (7/6)^2 = 1.3611; E: (9/6)^2 = 2.2500.
Sum of variances = 9.6111. Chain standard deviation = sqrt(9.6111) = 3.10 days. (Never add standard deviations directly.)

Step 4 — Governing deadline. The change request for 56 days was REJECTED by the change board, so the contractual 52-day deadline applies.

Step 5 — Probability of on-time completion:
z = (52 - 47.67)/3.10 = 1.40.
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 1.40) is approximately 0.919, so the probability of re-energising Hall C on time is about 91.9%.

Interpretation: the chain carries a healthy margin against the 52-day deadline, but activity C (tie-ins) contributes the largest variance and remains the best target for risk response if the estimates deteriorate.

For the canonical figures: the cumulative planned-value curve is week 1 = 100, week 2 = 250, week 3 = 450, week 4 = 700, week 5 = 900, week 6 = 1000, with AT = 4 and EV = 550.

Step 1 — Locate EV on the plan curve. Find the last week whose cumulative PV does not exceed EV: PV(3) = 450 <= 550 < PV(4) = 700, so ES lies between weeks 3 and 4.

Step 2 — Interpolate: ES = 3 + (EV - PV(3)) / (PV(4) - PV(3)) = 3 + (550 - 450) / (700 - 450) = 3 + 100/250 = 3 + 0.40 = 3.40 weeks.

Step 3 — Time-based schedule variance: SV(t) = ES - AT = 3.40 - 4 = -0.60 weeks. The negative sign means the project has earned only 3.40 weeks of planned work in 4 weeks of elapsed time — it is 0.60 weeks behind.

Step 4 — Time-based schedule performance index: SPI(t) = ES / AT = 3.40 / 4 = 0.85. The crew is delivering schedule progress at 85% of the planned rate.

Final answers: ES = 3.40 weeks; SV(t) = -0.60 weeks; SPI(t) = 0.85.

Step 1 — Expected duration per activity, te = (o + 4m + p) / 6:
A Isolate and drain chamber: (1 + 4x2 + 3)/6 = 12/6 = 2 days
B Cut out old valve set: (2 + 4x4 + 6)/6 = 24/6 = 4 days
C Install and weld new valve assembly: (2 + 4x5 + 8)/6 = 30/6 = 5 days
D Pressure test, disinfect, recommission: (1 + 4x3 + 5)/6 = 18/6 = 3 days

Step 2 — Expected chain duration: 2 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 14.00 days.

Step 3 — Activity standard deviations, sd = (p - o)/6, then sum variances:
A: (3-1)/6 = 1/3, variance 1/9
B: (6-2)/6 = 2/3, variance 4/9
C: (8-2)/6 = 1, variance 1
D: (5-1)/6 = 2/3, variance 4/9
Total variance = 1/9 + 4/9 + 9/9 + 4/9 = 18/9 = 2.00; chain standard deviation = sqrt(2.00) = 1.41 days.

Step 4 — Probability of finishing within the 16-day diversion window:
z = (deadline - expected) / sd = (16 - 14) / 1.4142 = 1.41.
From the standard normal distribution, P(Z <= 1.41) is approximately 0.9214, so prob_on_time is approximately 92.14%.

Answers: expected_duration = 14.00 days; std_dev = 1.41 days; prob_on_time = 92.14%.
